newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE-New NATO extends U.S. umbrella to happy few.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-New NATO extends U.S. umbrella to happy few.

text.p: The security architecture of Europe in the early 21st century will emerge from the drawing board at a summit of the NATO alliance in Madrid next week.

The 16-nation U.S.-led Atlantic alliance will offer membership to three former communist states of central Europe -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- while pledging to keep the door open for others in the future.

The July 8-9 summit will formalise the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's role as the paramount force for security on the continent well into the next century, following the European Union's failure in Amsterdam last month to make significant progress towards a common foreign and defence policy.

It will also discuss a reform of allied commands that should in theory make it easier for European allies to use NATO assets and headquarters to conduct their own operations in crises where the United States chooses not to get involved.

NATO leaders cleared the way for enlargement by signing the Founding Act of a new, cooperative relationship with Russia in Paris on May 27, blunting Moscow's continued hostility to its former satellites joining the western bloc.

Having created a NATO-Russia council to discuss European security problems, the West insists its expansion will extend a zone of stability eastwards, not draw new confrontation lines or create a security vacuum to the east.

But analysts differ over whether the decision to admit the most economically advanced and politically stable ex-members of the Warsaw Pact to NATO, eight years after the Berlin Wall's fall ended the Cold War, will guarantee more security in Europe.

"Madrid will be a step forward, but if it results only in admitting those east European countries that don't have security problems and leaving out those who do, and if there is no real shift of power within the alliance from the Americans to the Europeans, it will be a disappointment," a French official said.
EUROPEANS' FAILURE GIVES NATO PRIMACY

The French have long campaigned hardest for the Europeans to take their own security in hand, but they and the Germans failed to persuade the EU to become a defence organisation when it revised the Maastricht treaty on European union last month.
Atlanticist Britain and neutral Ireland, Sweden, Finland and Austria blocked Franco-German proposals to bring the Western European Union (WEU) defence grouping under the EU's orders.

"After Amsterdam, hopes of the EU moving very fast towards more cohesive security action have receded considerably. It will come in time through the WEU, but today NATO is the only game in town," said Simon Lunn, secretary-general of the North Atlantic Assembly, a grouping of NATO and east European parliamentarians.
The Madrid summit will perpetuate the American commitment to -- critics would say American dominance of -- European security despite the end of the Cold War.

Having failed to persuade Washington to hand over NATO's key southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to a European, France has decided to halt its return to the alliance's military wing, which it quit in 1966.

The west Europeans, still traumatised by their failure to prevent war in former Yugoslavia, cannot build a security system against the United States but only with it, says Dominique Moisi of the French Institute for International Relations.
The east Europeans, while looking to eventual EU membership for longer-term prosperity, are keen first and foremost to come under the American security umbrella, he said.
"They are more attracted to NATO than to the EU, if only because they know they can get in much quicker," Moisi said.

As for the Americans, despite questioning by isolationists of the cost and necessity of the new NATO, a majority of U.S. senators will see enlargement as "a sign that NATO is alive and moving forward and worthwhile", Lunn said.
Washington has reduced its troop presence in Europe from 250,000 in the Cold War to fewer than 100,000 today, but calls for a total pullout have found few backers.

"NATO is the instrument through which the United States remains engaged in Europe. The Europeans, especially the new central European members, will demonstrate in Madrid that they regard that engagement as vital," he added.
HOW EFFECTIVE IS NATO?
With no massive Soviet-style adversary to deter, NATO proved effective in bringing the war in Bosnia to an end in 1995 once the United States finally agreed to commit its own troops.

But its failure to intervene earlier, and the Europeans' ineffectual U.N. peacekeeping efforts, illustrated the increased risk of local wars in post-Cold War Europe without the restraining influence of the superpower standoff.
More recently, NATO held consultations but did not act when economically blighted Albania disintegrated into chaos this year, threatening renewed instability in the Balkans.

In that case, an ad hoc group of European allies led by Italy mounted a security force that tided the country over to democratic elections, although it has not disarmed heavily armed gangs who may be biding their time.

Although Western governments dare not admit it, there is no prospect of the alliance bringing in the Baltic republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania because that would deeply antagonise Russia, which regards them as part of its former Soviet Union security zone.
Nor has NATO been able or willing to end conflicts on the southern fringes of the former Soviet empire.

That raises the question of how useful the alliance would be in case of a blow-up between Russia and Ukraine, a war over Caspian Sea oil resources or a Moslem fundamentalist takeover somewhere in North Africa, three scenarios that worry strategists paid to gaze into crystal balls.
U.S. UNDER PRESSURE TO OPEN NATO DOOR AGAIN SOON

France and Italy led a majority of European allies who argue that adding Romania and Slovenia to the first wave of entrants would demonstrate NATO's commitment to security in the Black Sea and the Balkans, providing a wider deterrent.

The United States, concerned at the cost and possible Senate opposition, is insisting that only three central European states be admitted this time but is under strong pressure to pledge that the door will open again soon.

Western officials say NATO can bring greater stability to the whole of eastern Europe by giving countries that do not join now incentives to live as peaceful neighbours, settle minority or border issues, bring their armed forces under democratic control and cooperate with the West.
They point to the success of NATO's Partnership for Peace programmes of cooperation, information exchanges and joint military exercises with neutral and former communist states.
